extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (including corporate communicators and PR managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for practicing strategic public relations using an open-systems, two-way model that emphasizes sensing the environment, influencing and adapting organizational policy, and designing effective communication. Focus is on moving beyond reactive, craft-based publicity to research-driven, management-integrated PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open systems approach / two-way symmetric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should be cast in the role of bringing about mutual changes in both the environment and the organization as a result of environmental inputs; the open systems model uses 'two-way symmetric' approaches, meaning communication is two way and information exchange causes changes on both sides of organization–public relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implements reciprocal output–feedback adjustment; requires practitioners to sense the environment, be selectively sensitive to defined publics, initiate corrective actions, and seek outcomes that reflect mutual interests. Emphasis on mutual change rather than one-way persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid closed-systems / reactive / functionary PR
rubrics_metrics.description: A steady stream of news releases, email blasts, and other reactive responses suggests defensive, closed-systems thinking (functionary role) where PR supplies information only to the environment and not to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for assumptions: (1) PR's purpose is solely to change the environment, (2) persuasive communication alone will make changes happen, (3) media placements are all-powerful, (4) organizations need not change. Anti-patterns include focusing mainly on 'how things are said' and treating publicity/clippings as proof of communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR as advisory/part of top management (dominant coalition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who operate in the functional/open-systems mode become part of top management or the 'dominant coalition' and, when they have power there, can influence organizational ideology and choice of publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal is to move PR from a technician role to a communication counseling and management role, enabling influence on decision-making and organizational change rather than serving only in an advisory or output-producing capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful sensing and monitoring of the environment (research skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the open systems approach calls first and foremost for purposeful sensing of the environment to anticipate and detect changes that affect organizational relationships with publics; PR must have research skills to monitor publics and other environmental forces and forces within organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires measurement, analysis, and predictive modeling skills; portfolios should include measurement/analysis as well as writing; selective sensitivity to specifically defined publics; monitoring to detect issues before they become crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for proactive corrective action and crisis prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Open systems PR has the capacity to initiate corrective actions within organizations and direct programs to affect knowledge, predisposition, and behavior of both internal and external publics to maintain or achieve mutual-interest goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive corrective action taken in advance reduces both effort required and trauma associated with crisis-oriented reactive PR. Emphasize prevention and early adjustments rather than costly remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional (strategic) PR versus craft PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft PR treats PR as application of communication techniques aimed at getting publicity; professional PR relies on a body of knowledge and sees PR as strategic—managing conflict and building relationships with strategic publics that limit organizational autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor strategy, research, and management integration over mere technical output (clippings, media mentions). Training and education should move beyond journalistic output to management and measurement capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objectives: attention, interest, desire/intention, action
rubrics_metrics.description: The communication tasks in a crowded message environment: (1) get the attention of target publics, (2) stimulate interest in message content, (3) build a desire and intention to act on the message, (4) direct the action of those who behave consistent with the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages and media to clear each step; recognize fierce competition for attention and that many messages will be screened out by audiences (the 'obstinate audience').

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissemination is not the same as communication; required outcome steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending a message (dissemination) is not the same as communicating it. Evidence such as media placements or clippings does not prove communication has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess outcomes by the process steps of informing (attention, acceptance, interpretation as intended, storage), persuasion (adds accepting change), and instruction (adds stimulating active learning and practice). Use these steps as evaluation criteria rather than counts of placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source characteristics and credibility as initial receptivity factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of message sources affect receivers' initial acceptance (and sometimes long-term impact via sleeper effects); source credibility (status, reliability, expertness) amplifies the weight of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enhance message receptivity by selecting or developing credible sources; recognize that source effects vary by situation, topic, and time and mainly affect initial receptivity more than long-term impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message characteristics and receiver mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Meaning is in people, not words'—the same message may be interpreted differently by different receivers; message effects are mediated by receiver characteristics and situational variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messages to audience frames of reference and expect variability in interpretation; avoid assuming simple cause-effect rules—account for receiver variables in design and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium/channel selection and media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of medium matters: face-to-face interpersonal communication is historically most direct and powerful, but mediated formats (email, virtual meetings, digital channels) change interaction and provide cost/convenience benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select mediums based on desired interaction, immediacy of feedback, relationship intimacy, and context ('intimacy-transcends-distance'); combine media appropriately and understand how new technologies alter message dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience activity, selective attention, and the 'obstinate audience'
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences are exposed to thousands of messages daily and become choosy and resistant; many messages are screened out because of lack of interest, time, or preoccupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications that break through selective exposure—use targeting, relevance, and compelling openings; prioritize first getting attention before content objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of PR effects and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who must defend program strategy and budgets do so by their capacity to measure the effects of public relations programs on target publics; measurement and analysis are critical skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop metrics and evaluation approaches tied to outcomes (awareness, attitudes, behavior); include measurement competencies as part of professional development and to justify strategy and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment and adaptation model: communication quality insufficient without environmental interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjustment and adaptation model stipulates that quality of communication between organization and stakeholder publics is necessary but insufficient; practice must include capacity to monitor and interpret the organization's social environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theory to guide practice: couple communication quality with environmental scanning, interpretation, and strategic adaptation to create sustainable stakeholder relationships; emphasize building portfolios that demonstrate these capacities.
